blocks: Drag a breakpoint or segment to move it. Selected breakpoints move together.
Option-drag (Mac) / Alt-drag (Windows) a segment to curve it; double-click with the same modifier to straighten it.
Hold Shift while dragging to lock to one axis, or to fine-tune vertically.
Dragging a breakpoint horizontally over its neighbour removes the neighbour.
The grid is off by default in this tab and its settings are saved with the clip, separate from the other tabs. Turn it on with Snap to Grid or Cmd+4 (Mac) / Ctrl+4 (Windows).

Slide, Pressure, Velocity and Release Velocity envelopes can be scaled across the whole note: click outside the note, hover until the envelope turns blue, then drag up or down. Pitch can't be scaled this way.
Cmd+A / Ctrl+A on an envelope selects all its breakpoints so they can be shifted by the same amount.
Moving or stretching a note moves or stretches its expression with it.
Pitch breakpoints snap to the nearest semitone while holding Cmd (Mac) / Alt (Windows) with the grid off.
Pitch envelopes hide when Fold is on; Z zooms to fit the pitch bend in the time selection; Clear All Envelopes in the context menu removes a selected note's expression.
With Draw Mode on, drag freehand in the Pitch, Slide and Pressure lanes to draw an envelope.
Toggle Draw Mode with B, the Control Bar's Draw Mode switch, or the Options menu. Holding B turns it on only while held.
Shift while dragging gives finer values. With the grid on, drawing makes steps as wide as the visible grid; hold Cmd (Mac) / Alt (Windows) to draw on the grid while it is off.
12.4 MPE in Live’s Devices and on Push 2
Many of Live's own instruments support MPE and ship with MPE presets. They also respond to polyphonic aftertouch from Push 2; see Ableton/Live/UG/36 Push 2.
12.4 MPE in Live’s Devices and on Push 2
Live can read and modulate MPE data for plug-ins that support it.
A plug-in's MPE Mode on/off state is saved with its default configuration. Plug-ins with MIDI outputs can send MPE as well.

The MPE/Multi-channel Settings dialog sets up MPE output for hardware synths with particular zone needs, or for multi-timbral plug-ins that can be played from an MPE controller without official MPE support.
It opens from the Ext. Instrument device, from a MIDI track's I/O section in the mixer, or from the context menu of an MPE-enabled plug-in.
Ext. Instrument: pick a target in MIDI To, choose MPE in the second menu, then open that menu again and choose MPE Settings….
Mixer I/O section: with the target device chosen in the track's MIDI To, choose MPE in the second menu, then reopen it and choose MPE Settings…, in either the Session or Arrangement mixer.
Plug-ins: right-click the device's title bar.
The dialog chooses the MPE zone (lower or upper) and how many note channels it uses, or switches to multi-channel mode with any range of note channels.

Each zone has a global channel for controls that aren't per-note: channel 1 for the lower zone, channel 16 for the upper. The number of note channels sets the zone's polyphony, for example 1–11 for the lower zone and 12–16 for the upper.
A track outputs to one zone only, so using both zones takes two tracks. Zones apply only to MPE output.
Two tracks routed to the same MIDI output, one per zone, can drive two MPE synths chained through MIDI thru, or two sounds in one synth.
Commands that turn audio into MIDI: slicing, and converting harmony, melody or drums into a new MIDI track.
Besides warping, Live can pull musical information out of an audio clip and write it into a MIDI clip.
With an audio clip selected, the Create menu and the clip's context menu offer four commands: Slice to New MIDI Track, and Convert Harmony, Melody or Drums to New MIDI Track.
Slicing cuts the audio into pieces of time, one per MIDI note, without analysing pitch or rhythm. The pieces keep playing the original sound.
The dialog slices by beat division, by transients or by Warp Markers, and offers a Slicing Preset. A Rack holds at most 128 chains, so Live refuses settings that would make more than 128 slices.
Your own slicing presets go in the Defaults folder of the User Library.
The dialog slices by beat division, by transients or by Warp Markers, and offers a Slicing Preset. A Rack holds at most 128 chains, so Live refuses settings tha
Preserve warped timing keeps timing changes from warping; with it off, slices sound like the raw audio.
The dialog slices by beat division, by transients or by Warp Markers, and offers a Slicing Preset. A Rack holds at most 128 chains, so Live refuses settings tha
a new MIDI track with a clip holding one note per slice, in a rising chromatic sequence;
a Ableton/Instrument/Drum Rack on that track with one chain per slice, each a loaded with its slice;
the Drum Rack's controls mapped to envelope, loop and crossfade settings across every Simpler, as set by the slicing preset.
The sliced clip forms a rising "staircase" of notes. Editing the notes, or dragging Drum Rack pads onto each other to swap their notes, plays the slices in a new order.

Each slice has its own Drum Rack chain, so it can take its own audio effects. To share effects across several slices, select their chains and press Cmd+G (Mac) / Ctrl+G (Windows) to group them into a nested Rack, then add effects after it.
MIDI effects placed before the Drum Rack, such as Arpeggiator or Random, rearrange the slices as they play.
Slicing suits drum loops but also works on voices and ambient textures.

Live places note boundaries at the clip's transient markers, so adding, moving or deleting markers before converting tunes the result.
The "wrong" command can be useful: Convert Harmony on a monophonic vocal tends to add notes that weren't there.
The Groove Pool: applying a groove's timing and feel to clips and editing grooves.
Grooves change the timing and feel of a clip. Live's library grooves are Ableton/File/.agr files in the browser.
Drag a groove from the browser onto a clip to apply it. To audition several, turn on the Hot-Swap button above the clip's Clip Groove chooser and step through grooves while the clip plays.
Grooves work on MIDI clips and on audio clips; on audio they act through warping, so Warp must be on.
The Groove Pool holds every groove in use or loaded by double-clicking it in the browser. Grooves not used by any clip show greyed-out parameters.
Open it from the browser's view control menu, or with Cmd+Option+6 (Mac) / Ctrl+Alt+6 (Windows).
Each groove in the pool has buttons to save and hot-swap it, and these parameters, which change playback in real time:
Base — the note grid the groove is measured against, such as 1/4 or 1/8. Groove notes that fall on that grid don't move your notes.
Each groove in the pool has buttons to save and hot-swap it, and these parameters, which change playback in real time:
Quantize — straight quantization applied before the groove: 100% snaps to the Base grid, 0% leaves notes where they were.
Each groove in the pool has buttons to save and hot-swap it, and these parameters, which change playback in real time:
Timing — how strongly the groove's timing moves the clip.
Each groove in the pool has buttons to save and hot-swap it, and these parameters, which change playback in real time:
Random — random timing offsets, different for each voice; small amounts loosen tightly quantized loops.
Each groove in the pool has buttons to save and hot-swap it, and these parameters, which change playback in real time:
Velocity — how much the groove's velocities affect the clip, from −100 to +100. Negative values invert loud and quiet.
Each groove in the pool has buttons to save and hot-swap it, and these parameters, which change playback in real time:
Global Amount — scales Timing, Random and Velocity for every groove, up to 130%. It also appears in the Control Bar once any clip has a groove.
Each groove in the pool has buttons to save and hot-swap it, and these parameters, which change playback in real time:
Commit, above the Clip Groove chooser, writes the groove into the clip — moving MIDI notes, or adding Warp Markers to audio — and then sets the clip's groove to None.
What a groove does depends on its Groove Pool settings and on the note positions inside the groove file.
Drag a groove from the browser or Groove Pool onto a MIDI track to get its notes as an ordinary MIDI clip, edit them, then turn the clip back into a groove.
Drag any audio or MIDI clip into the Groove Pool, or choose Extract Groove from its context menu, to make a groove from its timing and volume.
Only the playing part of the clip counts.
Ways to get more from grooves.
A groove applies to a whole clip, so placing one drum voice behind the beat needs that voice in its own clip.
In a Drum or Instrument Rack, extract the chain for that voice (the snare, say) to its own track and clip, then give it a different groove.
Set a groove's Timing, Random and Velocity to 0% and use only Quantize and Base for quantization that can be changed or undone at any time. Which groove file you use then doesn't matter.
Duplicate a track, apply a groove with Random turned up to one copy, and play both: every note lands slightly apart from its twin, which thickens single string voices into a section.
Loading tuning systems other than twelve-tone equal temperament and how MIDI tracks follow them.
Live's default tuning is 12TET: twelve equal steps per octave. A tuning system can divide an octave, or a pseudo-octave that repeats at another interval, differently.
Live 12 loads Scala (.scl) files. The Core Library's tunings, under the Tunings label in the browser, use ASCL, Ableton's extension of the Scala format.
The Info View describes a tuning, including its notes per octave, when you hover over it in the browser or over a loaded tuning's name.
Your own .scl or .ascl files in any folder of Live's Places appear under the Tunings label with the User tag.

All of Live's built-in instruments follow a tuning system. MPE-enabled plug-ins and Max for Live instruments follow it when their pitch bend range is 48 semitones; other instruments will likely play out of tune.

Double-click a tuning file in the browser, or select it and press Enter, to load it. This opens the browser's Tuning section, which is hidden by default and can also be shown from the browser's view control menu.
.scl and .ascl files can also be dragged into the Tuning section from the computer. A loaded tuning is saved with the Live Set.
With a tuning loaded, the piano roll shows the tuning's notes instead of standard MIDI notes. Hovering over a note shows its pitch and frequency in the Status Bar.

Changing or removing a tuning leaves notes where they are, so they may now play different pitches. With Retune Set On Loading Tuning Systems on in the Options menu, Live moves notes to the closest pitches in the new tuning after a confirmation dialog.
Retuning can delete or shorten a note when two overlapping notes map to the same new pitch.
Changing or removing a tuning leaves notes where they are, so they may now play different pitches. With Retune Set On Loading Tuning Systems on in the Options m
While a tuning is loaded, the Scale Mode choosers disappear and scale-aware devices have Use Current Scale turned off.
The triangle next to the tuning's name expands settings for the reference pitch and the note range:
The triangle next to the tuning's name expands settings for the reference pitch and the note range:
Octave and Note — which note is the reference.
The triangle next to the tuning's name expands settings for the reference pitch and the note range:
Ref. Pitch/Freq — the reference frequency. Changing it raises or lowers every note in the Set.
The triangle next to the tuning's name expands settings for the reference pitch and the note range:
Lowest Note and Highest Note — what the lowest and highest notes play. Changing one moves the other, keeping the number of notes between them.
The triangle next to the tuning's name expands settings for the reference pitch and the note range:
Only Ref. Pitch/Freq changes the sound. Changing Octave or Note updates the displayed frequency without an audible jump until the frequency itself is changed.

The floppy disk button saves the tuning as an .ascl file to the Tunings label. The arrow next to it opens the tuning's page on Ableton's Tuning website, when one exists, with an editor for trying variations.
Select the tuning and press Delete to go back to 12TET.

Ableton's Tuning website explains the built-in tunings and has interactive tools for building and exporting your own. The ASCL specification describes how to write tuning files for Live.
How clips launch: launch modes, legato, launch quantization, velocity, nudging and Follow Actions.
In , how a clip behaves when launched shapes performance and improvisation. This chapter covers the per-clip launch settings.
Session View clips launch from their Clip Launch buttons or by remote control. Arrangement clips don't launch; they play at their place in the timeline, so these settings apply only to Session clips.
Double-click a Session clip to open Clip View, then choose the tab with the Clip Launch button icon.
Select several clips first to edit their launch settings together.
Launch Mode sets how a clip responds to mouse clicks, computer keys and MIDI notes:
Trigger — press starts the clip; release does nothing.
Launch Mode sets how a clip responds to mouse clicks, computer keys and MIDI notes:
Gate — press starts it; release stops it.
Launch Mode sets how a clip responds to mouse clicks, computer keys and MIDI notes:
Toggle — press starts it; the next press stops it.
Launch Mode sets how a clip responds to mouse clicks, computer keys and MIDI notes:
Repeat — while held, the clip retriggers at the clip quantization rate.
Launch Mode sets how a clip responds to mouse clicks, computer keys and MIDI notes:
A clip in Legato Mode takes over the play position of whatever clip was playing in its track, so you can switch between looping clips at any moment without losing sync, even with quantization off.
Useful for breaks: drop into an alternative loop and jump back.
Switching between clips that play different samples may drop out, because Live jumps to a part of the file it hasn't preloaded. Clip RAM Mode avoids this.
Clip Quantization corrects the launch timing of a clip. None turns it off; Global follows the Control Bar's Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar/Menu/Quantization.
Change global quantization with Cmd+6 to Cmd+0 (Mac) / Ctrl+6 to Ctrl+0 (Windows).
Any setting except None also quantizes launches made by Follow Actions.

Velocity Amount sets how much MIDI note velocity affects the clip's volume: at 0 it has no effect; at 100% the softest notes play silently. Playing clips from MIDI is covered in Ableton/Live/UG/34 MIDI and Key Remote.
The Nudge Backward and Forward buttons jump through a playing clip by the global quantization amount.
They can be mapped to keys or MIDI. In MIDI Map Mode a scrub control appears between them, which suits a rotary encoder for continuous scrubbing.
With quantization under one bar, launching, nudging or scrubbing can shift a clip away from Live's master clock.

A Follow Action decides what happens next in a clip's group after it plays. A group is the run of clips in adjacent slots of one track; empty slots separate groups. Scenes have Follow Actions too, in the Scene View.
Follow Action button — turns Follow Actions on for the selected clip or scene; off by default; Shift+Enter.
Follow Action A and B — two actions to choose between.
Chance A and Chance B — the relative probability of each. A at 100% and B at 0% always picks A; raising B to 90% makes A happen about one launch in ten. The slider between them adjusts both.
Linked/Unlinked (clips only) — Linked fires at the end of the clip, or after the number of loops in the Multiplier field. Unlinked fires after the Follow Action Time.
Follow Action Time — bars-beats-sixteenths from where play starts; one bar by default. A draggable marker shows it in the clip editor.
No Action — nothing happens, and once chosen, the other action no longer gets a chance.
Stop — stops the clip after the Follow Action Time, overriding its loop settings.
Next — plays the clip below, wrapping from the last to the first.
First and Last — play the top or bottom clip of the group.
Any — plays any clip in the group.
Other — like Any, but never repeats the current clip while there are others.
Jump — plays a chosen slot or scene, set with the Jump Target slider.
Clips and scenes with Follow Actions show a striped launch button.
Follow Actions bypass global quantization but respect clip quantization other than None or Global.

The Enable Follow Actions Globally button, next to Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View/Button/Back to Arrangement, turns every Follow Action in the Set on or off, which is handy for editing a running clip. It is greyed out when the Set has none.
Clip Follow Actions keep running when a scene Follow Action is scheduled, but scene Follow Actions win once they fire.
Follow Actions let loop-based music repeat yet still surprise; recording the results gives new material.
To play a long clip once and then loop only its last eight bars:
In Arrangement View, with Loop off, use Edit → Split to cut the clip where the loop should start.
To play a long clip once and then loop only its last eight bars:
Drag both pieces into adjacent slots of one Session track, forming a group.
To play a long clip once and then loop only its last eight bars:
On the first clip set Follow Action Time to its length, Action A to Next at 100%, and Action B to No Action.
To play a long clip once and then loop only its last eight bars:
Turn Loop on for the second clip.
To play a long clip once and then loop only its last eight bars:
Give every clip or scene in a group the Next action and they play in a cycle until stopped. Adding Any at a low Chance occasionally reshuffles it.
Create Follow Action Chain in a clip's context menu loops all selected clips, which needn't be adjacent.
A single clip with Play Again at 80% and No Action at 20%, and a one-bar Follow Action Time, repeats its first bar a few times before playing on through the rest of the sample.
Or play a clip to a set point and then Next into a looping copy of the same file, which itself can loop forever, for a while, or until chance moves on.
Randomly triggering clips that differ only in clip envelopes or warp settings gives small variations, such as changing pitch bend, effects or transposition.

Identical melody clips in Legato Mode can hand over to each other without the melody changing; editing each clip's settings, envelopes or notes a little at a time then makes the melody change gradually.

Make several copies of a beat or melody with different start and end points and envelopes, set each Follow Action Time to the length you want played, give each two actions with different Chances, and launch one for an unpredictable remix.
Clips with odd Follow Action Times interact so they seldom play in the same order or position, which suits sound installations meant to run for weeks without repeating themselves.
Track inputs and outputs: monitoring, external audio and MIDI, resampling and routing between tracks.
Routing sets each track's signal source and destination. Most of it happens in the mixer's In/Out section, Live's patchbay.
Show or hide In/Out from the mixer's view control menu at the bottom right, from View → Mixer Controls → In/Out, or with Ctrl+Option+I (Mac) / Ctrl+Alt+I (Windows).
Every clip-playing track has the same layout:
Audio/MIDI From — the input. Return tracks take their input from their sends.
Every clip-playing track has the same layout:
Monitor — when the input is heard through the track.
Every clip-playing track has the same layout:
Audio/MIDI To — the output. Every track outputs audio except MIDI tracks with no instrument.
Every clip-playing track has the same layout:
In each chooser pair, the upper Type chooser picks a category (such as Ext. for an audio or MIDI interface) and the lower Channel chooser picks a specific input, output or channel within it.
Monitoring passes a track's input to its output through the device chain, so you hear what you play, with effects and interface latency.
Each audio and MIDI track has three monitor modes:
Auto (Ableton/Track/IO/Monitor/Auto) — monitors while the track is armed, but not while it plays clips. Suits most recording.
Each audio and MIDI track has three monitor modes:
In — always monitors the input and silences the track's clips, turning it into an aux-style input. The track's Activator switch turns blue to show it.
Each audio and MIDI track has three monitor modes:

Off (Ableton/Track/IO/Monitor/Off) — never monitors. For acoustic instruments heard in the room, an external mixer, or an interface's direct monitoring. Set Overall Latency in the Audio Settings when recording this way.
Each audio and MIDI track has three monitor modes:

With In or Auto, Keep Monitoring Latency in Recorded Audio is on by default, lining the recording up with what you heard. Leave it on for software instruments and effects; turn it off for acoustic instruments or external monitoring. Right-click the In or Auto button to switch it.
Clicking a Monitor button applies to all selected tracks. With In/Out shown, Delete or Edit → Return to Default resets it: Off for audio tracks, Auto for MIDI tracks.

Choose Ext. In as an audio track's Input Type to use the interface's inputs; the Input Channel chooser lists them with level meters that flash red on overload. Outputs work the same way. Changes apply to all selected tracks.
The Configure… entry opens the Audio Settings, whose Channel Configuration dialogs choose which interface inputs and outputs Live uses and whether they are mono or stereo pairs.
Channels can be renamed in those dialogs (Tab moves between them); the names show in the choosers and belong to that audio device.
A mono input records mono samples; anything else records stereo. Inside the device chain the signal is always stereo.
Mono becomes stereo by copying the signal to both sides. Routing to a mono output sums left and right and lowers the result 6 dB to avoid clipping.
See also Ableton/Track/Q/How can I turn a mono signal into stereo in a channel?

A MIDI track's Input Type chooser picks one MIDI port or All Ins, the merge of every port. Input Channel picks one channel or All Channels, with activity meters on each entry. Changes apply to all selected MIDI tracks.
Settings → Link, Tempo & MIDI lists every MIDI input and output port. Each can be used by any number of tracks.
Sends or receives notes and CC messages.
Turn it on for an input to play or record notes, or to record CC from a hardware synth into clips.
Turn it on for an output to play external hardware, send notes to another app through a virtual MIDI bus, or send CC automation out.
A controller's output port needs Track only if the controller makes its own sound.
Sends or receives MIDI Clock, or receives MIDI Timecode. A controller needs it only if it has a sequencer or arpeggiator.
Input: to follow an external sequencer, drum machine, groovebox or another DAW. Output: to drive those from Live, or to sync an external synth's LFO and arpeggiator.
Expanding an output port with Sync on shows more options:
MIDI Clock Sync Delay — delays outgoing sync in milliseconds to fix timing offsets.
Expanding an output port with Sync on shows more options:
MIDI Clock Type — Song sends Song Position Pointer and Continue whenever the play position changes; Pattern sends only Start, at the next bar, for devices that ignore SPP.
Expanding an output port with Sync on shows more options:
Hardware Resync — what the Control Bar's Resync External Hardware button sends to bring synced gear that has fallen out of time back in line: Stop and Start (default), Start Only, or Don't Resync.
Expanding an output port with Sync on shows more options:
Lets a controller map to Live's parameters, and sends feedback back to it.
Input: for custom MIDI mappings, or to launch clips from a keyboard. Launchpad/Custom/Mode/1 Arrangement needs Remote on for the Launchpad's input.
Output: for controllers whose LEDs or motorised faders show the state of mapped parameters.
